questions.stem: One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals:
questions.explanation: The radian is defined by arc length: an arc equal to the radius subtends 1 radian, so a full turn is 2π radians. An arc of 1/360 of the circumference subtends 1 degree.

questions.stem: An angle of 150° in radians is:
questions.explanation: Multiply by π/180: 150 × π/180 = 5π/6. The value 3π/4 is 135° and 2π/3 is 120°.

questions.stem: An angle of 7π/4 radians in degrees is:
questions.explanation: Multiply by 180/π: (7/4) × 180° = 315°. The value 225° is 5π/4.

questions.stem: An angle of 2 radians, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: 2 × 180/π ≈ 114.6°. The value 57.3° is one radian, and 0.03° comes from multiplying by π/180, the conversion the other way.

questions.stem: An arc of a circle of radius 6 cm subtends an angle of 2π/3 at the centre. The arc length is:
questions.explanation: Arc length is l = rθ with θ in radians: 6 × 2π/3 = 4π cm. The value 12π is the sector area (1/2)r²θ, a different quantity.

questions.stem: An arc of length 15 cm lies on a circle of radius 10 cm. The angle it subtends at the centre is:
questions.explanation: From l = rθ, θ = 15/10 = 1.5 radians. Dividing the radius by the arc length gives 0.67, and the result of l/r is in radians, not degrees.

questions.stem: The tip of an 80 cm pendulum swings through an angle of 30°. The length of the arc it travels, to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: Convert first: 30° = π/6. Then l = 80 × π/6 ≈ 41.9 cm. Using 30 directly in l = rθ gives 2400 cm, because the formula needs radians.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite an angle of 30° is 4 cm long. The hypotenuse is:
questions.explanation: sin 30° = opposite/hypotenuse = 1/2, so the hypotenuse is 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8 cm. Multiplying by sin 30° gives 2 cm, and 4√3 cm is the adjacent side.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, angle A = 40°, angle B = 65° and side a = 12 cm, where a is opposite A. Side b, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: By the sine rule, b/sin B = a/sin A, so b = 12 sin 65°/sin 40° ≈ 16.92 cm. Inverting the ratio gives 8.51 cm, and 18.03 cm uses angle C = 75° instead of B.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 5 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 60°. The third side is:
questions.explanation: By the cosine rule, c² = 5² + 8² − 2 × 5 × 8 × cos 60° = 89 − 40 = 49, so c = 7 cm. Adding the last term gives √129, and dropping the 2 gives √69.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 7 cm, 8 cm and 13 cm. The largest angle is:
questions.explanation: The largest angle is opposite 13: cos C = (49 + 64 − 169)/(2 × 7 × 8) = −56/112 = −1/2, so C = 120°. Losing the negative sign gives 60°.

questions.stem: In triangle PQR, angle P = 30°, angle Q = 105° and side PQ = 10 m. Side QR, opposite P, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: Angle R = 180° − 30° − 105° = 45°, and PQ is opposite R. Then QR = 10 sin 30°/sin 45° ≈ 7.07 m. Using sin 105° gives 13.66 m, which is side PR.

questions.stem: A point P on the unit circle is at angle θ measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. The coordinates of P are:
questions.explanation: The unit circle definitions are cos θ = x-coordinate and sin θ = y-coordinate of P. Swapping them would put the point for θ = 0 at (0, 1).

questions.stem: Using the unit circle definitions, tan θ equals:
questions.explanation: tan θ is the gradient of the radius to P, y/x = sin θ/cos θ, defined when cos θ ≠ 0. The reciprocal cos θ/sin θ is undefined at θ = 0, where tan 0 = 0.

questions.stem: For an angle θ with π/2 < θ < π, which is true?
options: sin θ > 0, cos θ < 0, tan θ < 0
sin θ < 0, cos θ > 0, tan θ < 0
sin θ > 0, cos θ > 0, tan θ > 0
sin θ > 0, cos θ < 0, tan θ > 0
questions.explanation: In the second quadrant the point on the unit circle has x < 0 and y > 0, so cos θ < 0 and sin θ > 0. Then tan θ = sin θ/cos θ is negative.

questions.stem: For every real number x, sin²x + cos²x equals:
questions.explanation: The point (cos x, sin x) lies on the unit circle x² + y² = 1, so sin²x + cos²x = 1 for every x.

questions.stem: If sin x = 3/5 and π/2 < x < π, then cos x is:
questions.explanation: cos²x = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, so cos x = ±4/5. In the second quadrant cosine is negative, so cos x = −4/5. The value 2/5 subtracts sin x from 1 without squaring.

questions.stem: If cos x = −5/13 and π < x < 3π/2, then tan x is:
questions.explanation: sin²x = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169, and sine is negative in the third quadrant, so sin x = −12/13. Then tan x = (−12/13)/(−5/13) = 12/5, positive in the third quadrant.

questions.stem: The expression 3 − 3sin²x simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Factorise: 3(1 − sin²x) = 3cos²x, using sin²x + cos²x = 1. The 3 is a common factor, so it is not squared.

questions.stem: The exact value of cos(π/6) is:
questions.explanation: π/6 is 30°, and in the 30°-60°-90° triangle the side adjacent to 30° is √3 when the hypotenuse is 2, so cos(π/6) = √3/2. The value 1/2 is sin(π/6).

questions.stem: The exact value of sin(5π/4) is:
questions.explanation: 5π/4 = π + π/4 lies in the third quadrant, where sine is negative, so sin(5π/4) = −sin(π/4) = −√2/2.

questions.stem: The exact value of cos(2π/3) is:
questions.explanation: 2π/3 = π − π/3 is in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative, so cos(2π/3) = −cos(π/3) = −1/2. The value −√3/2 uses sin(π/3) instead.

questions.stem: The exact value of tan(5π/3) is:
questions.explanation: 5π/3 = 2π − π/3 is in the fourth quadrant, where tangent is negative, so tan(5π/3) = −tan(π/3) = −√3. The value −1/√3 is −tan(π/6).

questions.stem: The exact value of sin(11π/6) + cos(4π/3) is:
questions.explanation: sin(11π/6) = −sin(π/6) = −1/2 (fourth quadrant) and cos(4π/3) = −cos(π/3) = −1/2 (third quadrant). The sum is −1. Getting one sign wrong gives 0.

questions.stem: For all x, sin(π + x) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Adding π moves the point to the opposite side of the unit circle, changing the sign of both coordinates, so sin(π + x) = −sin x. The sine keeps its sign for π − x, not π + x.

questions.stem: For all x, cos(2π − x) is equal to:
questions.explanation: The angle 2π − x is the reflection of x in the x-axis, which keeps the x-coordinate, so cos(2π − x) = cos x. The y-coordinate changes sign, so sin(2π − x) = −sin x.

questions.stem: For all x where it is defined, tan(π + x) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Both sin and cos change sign under x → π + x, so their quotient is unchanged: tan(π + x) = tan x. This is why tan has period π.

questions.stem: Given sin a = 0.6, the value of sin(π − a) + sin(π + a) is:
questions.explanation: sin(π − a) = sin a = 0.6 and sin(π + a) = −sin a = −0.6, so the sum is 0. Treating both as +sin a gives 1.2.

questions.stem: Given cos t = 0.3, the value of cos(π − t) − cos(2π + t) is:
questions.explanation: cos(π − t) = −cos t = −0.3, and cos(2π + t) = cos t = 0.3 by periodicity. So the expression is −0.3 − 0.3 = −0.6.

questions.stem: The periods of y = sin x and y = tan x are:
questions.explanation: Sine repeats after a full turn, 2π. Tangent repeats after half a turn, π, because tan(π + x) = tan x.

questions.stem: On the domain −2π ≤ x ≤ 2π, the x-intercepts of y = sin x are at exactly:
questions.explanation: sin x = 0 at every integer multiple of π, and five of these lie in the domain, including the endpoints. The odd multiples of π/2 are the x-intercepts of y = cos x.

questions.stem: On the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, the graph of y = cos x is below the x-axis for:
questions.explanation: cos x is the x-coordinate on the unit circle, which is negative in the second and third quadrants, π/2 < x < 3π/2. The interval π < x < 2π is where sin x is negative.

questions.stem: The graph of y = 3 sin 2x has:
questions.explanation: For y = a sin bx, the amplitude is |a| = 3 and the period is 2π/b = 2π/2 = π. Multiplying 2π by 2 gives 4π, the period of sin(x/2).

questions.stem: The graph of y = −2 cos(x/2) has:
options: amplitude 2, period 4π, reflected in the x-axis
amplitude 2, period π, reflected in the x-axis
amplitude 1/2, period 4π, reflected in the x-axis
questions.explanation: The amplitude is |−2| = 2, the period is 2π ÷ 1/2 = 4π, and the negative sign reflects the graph in the x-axis so it starts at a minimum of −2. Using 2π × 1/2 gives π.

questions.stem: The range of y = 4 sin 3x is:
questions.explanation: sin 3x takes every value from −1 to 1, and multiplying by 4 dilates this to −4 to 4. The 3 changes the period, not the range.

questions.stem: The function f(x) = 2 sin(x/3) has domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 3π. Its range is:
questions.explanation: As x runs from 0 to 3π, x/3 runs from 0 to π, where sine goes from 0 up to 1 and back to 0. So f takes values 0 to 2. The full range −2 to 2 would need a whole period, 6π.

questions.stem: A graph of the form y = a cos bx, with b > 0, has a maximum of 5 at x = 0 and a period of π/2. The values of a and b are:
questions.explanation: The maximum at x = 0 gives a = 5. The period is 2π/b = π/2, so b = 4. Taking b = 1/4 would give period 8π.

questions.stem: A graph of the form y = a sin bx, with b > 0, has amplitude 3, period 6π, and y < 0 just to the right of x = 0. The values of a and b are:
questions.explanation: Going below the axis just after the origin means a reflection in the x-axis, so a = −3. The period 2π/b = 6π gives b = 1/3. Using b = 3 gives period 2π/3.

questions.stem: The period of y = tan 3x is:
questions.explanation: y = tan bx has period π/b, so the period is π/3. Using 2π/b, the rule for sine and cosine, gives 2π/3.

questions.stem: On the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ π, the vertical asymptotes of y = tan 2x are at:
options: x = 0, x = π/2 and x = π
questions.explanation: tan 2x is undefined when 2x = π/2 or 3π/2, so x = π/4 or 3π/4. The values 0, π/2 and π are where tan 2x = 0, its x-intercepts.
